title: Beta-multiplier bias
description: The constant-$g_m$ (beta-multiplier) self-biased reference. In the full circuit a top PMOS current mirror forces equal currents down two legs; the bottom devices are a diode-connected small device and a K-times-wider device with a source resistor $R_{bias}$. Because both carry the same current but the wide device runs at a lower current density, the wide device needs less gate-source voltage, and the difference is dropped across $R_{bias}$. Setting that up makes the reference's transconductance depend only on the resistor and the ratio, not on the current or the process: the square-law hand identity is $g_m = (2/R_{bias})*(1 - 1/\sqrt{K_{bm}})$. This sheet draws the bottom pair and its resistor, not the top mirror. The wide device is given the diode device's current, the equality the top mirror enforces; its drain is held at $V_{dm2}$, the level the top mirror would set; and the diode device's node, the gate wire both bottom devices share, is a port, because the current the top mirror delivers into it arrives from outside the sheet. Like a Widlar, the loop is a fixed point with one unknown, and the sheet solves it: you pick the resistor, the ratio and the diode device's inversion level, and the engine searches $I_{bias}$ between its min and max for the current at which the gate-source difference equals $I_{bias}*R_{bias}$. It is one named unknown searched in a stated range, not a nodal solve; the fixed-point check reports the identity the search makes hold, and the search range starts above zero, so it finds the operating state and never the zero-current one. The $g_m$ identity is an advisory check, an estimate, because it comes from the square-law model while the lookup $g_m$ is the truth; it shows how far the classic formula is off at this inversion level. The circuit has a second, zero-current stable state, so a startup subcircuit is required in practice; it is a simulation-only concern and is not sized here. The resistor-side device's source sits $I_{bias}*R_{bias}$ above ground, declared as its $V_{SB}$.

params.name: I_bias
params.note: loop current in each leg, set by the resistor and the ratio: the current at which the gate-source step from the diode device to the resistor-side device equals the drop that current develops across R_bias. Solved, not set: the engine searches for it between min and max, so the stored value is never read

params.name: K_bm
params.note: width ratio of the resistor-side device to the diode device; larger K raises gm for a given resistor

params.name: R_bias
params.note: the bias resistor; sets the reference transconductance

params.name: V_dm2
params.note: drain DC level of the resistor-side device (set by the top mirror). Stated by the designer: the top current mirror that sets it is not on this sheet

doc.title: Diode device (small)
doc.description: The diode-connected side of the bottom pair, carrying the loop current. Its transconductance is the one the constant-$g_m$ identity predicts, and its gate-source voltage is the level of the gate wire the two bottom devices share; the wide device's gate-source voltage sits below it by the resistor drop.

equations.name: gm_target
equations.note: square-law constant-gm identity; an estimate the LUT gm is checked against

equations.name: delta_vgs
equations.note: the actual gate-source step from the diode device to the resistor-side device

equations.name: vgs_drop
equations.note: the gate-source step the resistor develops at the loop current

checks.note: the resistor-side operating point must stay within the data's weak-inversion ceiling
the constant-gm loop equation V_GS1 - V_GS2 = I_bias*R_bias. The search on I_bias makes it hold, so this check is the identity that search solves: it fails only where the search did not settle
the classic square-law gm = (2/R)(1 - 1/sqrt(K)); the LUT gm is the truth, so this shows how far the hand formula drifts at this inversion. Estimate-grade
